memoryText: Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Deuteronomy 6:4-5 is the unit’s anchor verse. It is the greatest commandment, and the center of the book that you have just finished reading. Read it aloud once more before you continue.

“Hear, O Israel.” The word “hear” in Hebrew is shema, and it means to listen and obey. After forty years of failing to listen, Israel is told again to hear. This is the way that every part of the covenant begins. Faith comes by hearing.

“The LORD our God, the LORD is one.” There is one God. There is no rival, no partner, and no competing power. He is the LORD, the covenant name given at the burning bush. And he is “our God,” bound to his people in love. The oneness of God is the foundation of Israel’s life, and of the Christian faith.

“You shall love the LORD your God.” The commandment is to love. This is not a request for mere compliance. The whole law, the sacrifices, the festivals, the justice, is meant to be the expression of love for God. Moses told the people many times in this book that obedience should flow from love.

“With all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might.” The love is to be total. Heart is the center of thought and will. Soul is the whole self, life itself. Might is strength, resources, energy. Nothing is held back. Jesus added “mind” when he quoted the verse (Mark 12:30), but the sense is the same: everything we are belongs to God.

For the Christian, the verse is both a command and a promise. We cannot keep it on our own. But God promised in Deuteronomy 30:6 that he would circumcise our hearts so that we would love him. In Christ, that promise is fulfilled. The Spirit pours God’s love into our hearts (Romans 5:5), and we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).
unitRecap:
In Unit 7 you have read the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy, the forty years in the wilderness and the sermons of Moses that prepared Israel for the land. You began with the census at Sinai and saw the camp arranged around the tabernacle, with the Levites set apart as substitutes for the firstborn. You read the blessing that God told Aaron to speak over his people, and Psalm 90, Moses’ prayer about the brevity of life and the eternity of God.

You followed Israel as it left Sinai with the cloud above and the ark in front, and you saw the march break down in complaining. You read the story of the twelve spies and the decision of the people not to enter the land, and the sentence of forty years. You prayed Psalm 95 and heard its warning, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” You read of Korah’s rebellion, Aaron’s budding staff, and the red heifer, and of Moses’ sin at the rock and the bronze serpent that healed those who looked. You heard the oracles of Balaam and the promise of a star from Jacob.

You read of the second generation. They fell at Baal of Peor, were numbered again, and received Joshua as their leader. You read the offerings and the vows, the war against Midian, the stages of the journey, the boundaries of the land, and the cities of refuge, whose manslayers were freed by the death of the high priest.

Then Moses began to preach. He looked back at the journey and told the people that God had carried them as a man carries his son. He restated the Ten Commandments and gave the Shema, the greatest commandment. He told Israel that God’s choice was not because of their righteousness, and he retold the golden calf. You paused to study the three offices of Christ as prophet, priest, and king. You read the law of the king and the promise of a prophet like Moses. You read the many laws of justice and mercy, the creed of the firstfruits, the covenant at Ebal and Gerizim, and the blessings and curses. Moses called Israel to choose life, taught them the Song of the Rock, blessed the tribes, and died on Mount Nebo. All along, you prayed through Psalm 78, which told the story as a lesson for children, and Psalm 119, which praised the word of God.

The unit taught that unbelief is the root of rebellion, that God is patient and faithful, that the heart must be changed by God, and that the whole of the law is to be summed up in love.

reviewQuestions.question: What does Israel’s wilderness rebellion reveal about the human heart?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Look back at the spies (Numbers 13 and 14), Korah (Numbers 16), and Psalm 95. Consider what Moses says in Deuteronomy 29:4 about the heart. Ask what Israel needed that miracles could not give.

reviewQuestions.question: What is the structure of Deuteronomy, and why does it matter that it resembles a covenant treaty?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Recall the pattern: a historical review (chapters 1 to 4), the commandments (5 to 26), the blessings and curses (27 to 30), and the arrangements for the future (31 to 34). Think about why God would bind his people with a covenant instead of only commanding.

reviewQuestions.question: What does Moses mean by the blessings and curses in Deuteronomy 27 and 28?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Review Deuteronomy 28:1-14 and 28:15-68, and the reason in 28:47. Read Galatians 3:10-14, and consider how the curses were fulfilled in Israel’s history and in Christ.

reviewQuestions.question: How does Moses function as a type of Christ, and where does he fall short?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Think about Moses as prophet, mediator, intercessor, and leader. Consider Numbers 20, Deuteronomy 18:15, and Deuteronomy 34:10. Read Hebrews 3:1-6 and ask what the Son does that the servant could not.

prayerPrompts: Thank God for carrying you through these years of wilderness and patience.
Thank him for Christ as prophet, priest, and king.
Ask him to keep the unit verse before you.
